activities.anchor: Nothing is hollow or clever about it
activities.caption: shell, frame or mass? file each structure
activities.name: slFamilySort

config.prompt: Three families, natural and manufactured — file each:
config.why: Classification is a lens, not a box — the same house is mass at its foundation, frame in its skeleton and shell in its roof.

activities.anchor: and we associate it with bridges and towers
activities.caption: flat vs pleated — drag the divider
activities.name: slPaperCompare

config.prompt: The schoolroom classic — drag between the two states:

before.label: Flat sheet
before.text: Lies limp across a 15 cm gap — the material is fine; the shape is doing no work.

after.label: Pleated sheet
after.text: The same sheet, folded, carries a stack of coins — the folds act like tiny I-beams, moving material to where bending stress lives.

config.why: Materials supply strength; shape decides how that strength is used — an eggshell outperforms a flat steel plate of the same weight across the same span.

activities.anchor: the fatigue problem that grounds aircraft parts and cracks old bridges
activities.caption: call the static load
activities.name: slStandEst

config.prompt: A 60 kg person standing still on a platform loads it with about how many newtons?
config.why: About 590 N (60 × 9.81) — but the same person jumping onto it can momentarily load it with 2,000 N or more: impact multiplies force.
config.context: Dynamic loads also repeat — a member that survives one gust may fail after a million of them.

activities.anchor: a bridge swaying at its own natural frequency
activities.caption: bet before the reveal — what wobbled the bridge?
activities.name: slMillenniumPredict

config.q: The London Millennium Bridge opened in 2000 and wobbled shut within days. What loaded it?
choices: Overload — more pedestrians than the static design allowed
Synchronised footsteps — a dynamic load the designers had modelled as static sideways pushes
config.why: Not overload: structure failure depends on time as well as size — arriving fast, moving, and repeated, dynamic loads stress differently than the number on a scale.

activities.caption: pair each force with its everyday case
activities.name: slForceMatch

config.prompt: Five forces attack every structure — pair each with its case:

pairs.right: the cable of a crane hook, the string of a drawn bow
table legs, the stone columns of a temple
scissors through paper, a rivet joining two overlapping plates

pairs.left: bending — stretches one face, squeezes the other
pairs.right: a loaded shelf with a neutral middle doing little
a screwdriver shaft under load, a wrung-out towel

config.why: In pure tension or compression a material uses its full strength efficiently — which is why good structures try to stay in the gentle pair.

activities.anchor: the moment the shelf or beam must survive
activities.caption: find the faulty line — forces with numbers
activities.name: slWireSpot

config.prompt: One of these load-path claims is backwards — click it:
lines: A 12 kg sign hangs from a steel wire, so the wire carries about 118 N.
In pure tension or pure compression, a material uses its full strength efficiently.
A screwdriver transmitting 20 N at a 15 mm radius carries a twisting moment of 0.3 N·m.
The wire carries the sign's weight only near the top; the bottom half carries none.
A narrow blade concentrates the twisting moment.
config.correction: Tension runs the whole path: every cross-section of the wire carries the same ~118 N, top to bottom.
config.why: A structure is a load path — the force entering one end travels through every member between it and the ground.

config.prompt: Real shelving calls for a bracket at roughly what spacing, rather than trusting the material?
config.why: About 60 cm — the bending moment tracks load AND span, which is why long unsupported shelves sag while short ones do not.

activities.anchor: with every diagonal either pulling (a tie, in tension) or pushing (a strut, in compression)
activities.caption: true or false — reinforcement by geometry
activities.name: slTriangJudge

statements.s: A rectangle of four members can lean into a parallelogram without any member changing length.
statements.why: Which is why gates sag and scaffolding sways — until a diagonal locks the geometry.

statements.s: A triangle cannot deform without one of its members stretching or squashing.
statements.why: And members are built to resist exactly that — the whole of structural engineering hides in the observation.

statements.s: Corrugation stiffens a sheet by adding material to it.
statements.why: By moving it — the folds act like tiny I-beams, moving material away from the neutral middle to the faces.

statements.s: Corrugated cardboard's fluted middle layer holds the two flat liners apart.
statements.why: A sandwich of weak paper converted into a stiff panel that ships the world's goods.
